about: Stress Analysis 1 (MECH40005) is a core Year 1 module on Imperial's MEng Mechanical Engineering, running across the year. It introduces stress, strain and Hooke's law, the elastic constants (Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio), and applies them to forces in plane frames, thin-walled pressure vessels and beams. The topics follow the list recorded from the department's module descriptor (which could not be re-read when this pack was written) and a 2021-22 third-party course summary, with beams split into shear force and bending moment, bending stress and deflection. Assessment details could not be confirmed, so check the department's module page.
topics: Stress, strain, Hooke's law and Poisson's ratio
Elastic moduli and axially loaded members
Shear force and bending moment in beams

notes.body:
A plane frame (truss) is a set of straight bars joined at their ends to form triangles. In the idealised model used in a first course:
- joints are frictionless pins, so a bar cannot carry a moment;
- loads are applied only at the joints;
- self-weight is ignored or lumped at the joints.
Each bar is then a two-force member: it carries a single axial force, either tension (pulling on the joints) or compression (pushing on them). Convention: assume every unknown force is tensile; a negative answer means compression.

Static determinacy
For a plane pin-jointed frame with m members, r independent reaction components and j joints, each joint gives two equilibrium equations, so:
- m + r = 2j: statically determinate (forces found from equilibrium alone), provided the frame is properly arranged;
- m + r > 2j: statically indeterminate (redundant members; you also need compatibility and member stiffness);
- m + r < 2j: a mechanism.
The count is necessary but not sufficient: a badly arranged frame can satisfy it and still collapse.

Method of joints
1. Find the support reactions from equilibrium of the whole frame (ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0).
2. Start at a joint with no more than two unknown bar forces.
3. Resolve ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at that joint, then move on.
Example: a triangle with supports at A (pin) and B (roller) 4 m apart and apex C 2 m above the mid-point, carrying 10 kN down at C. By symmetry each reaction is 5 kN upward. At A the bar AC is at 45°: vertical equilibrium gives F_AC sin 45° + 5 = 0, so F_AC = −7.07 kN (compression). Horizontal equilibrium gives F_AB + F_AC cos 45° = 0, so F_AB = +5 kN (tension).

Method of sections
Cut the frame through no more than three bars whose forces are unknown, and apply equilibrium to one part. Taking moments about the point where two of the cut bars meet gives the third directly.
Example: a Warren truss of equilateral triangles with 2 m sides (height √3 ≈ 1.732 m) spans 6 m between a pin at A and a roller at D, with bottom joints B and C at 2 m and 4 m. A 12 kN load acts at B, so R_A = 8 kN and R_D = 4 kN. Cut through top chord EF, diagonal BF and bottom chord BC:
- moments about F (x = 3 m, top): F_BC × 1.732 = 8 × 3 − 12 × 1, so F_BC = 6.93 kN (tension);
- moments about B: F_EF × 1.732 = −8 × 2, so F_EF = −9.24 kN (compression);
- vertical forces: 8 − 12 + F_BF sin 60° = 0, so F_BF = 4.62 kN (tension).

Useful shortcuts
- At an unloaded joint where only two non-collinear bars meet, both are zero-force members.
- At an unloaded joint with three bars, two of them collinear, the third bar carries zero force.
- Top chords of simply supported trusses under downward loads are in compression; bottom chords in tension.

Exam tips: draw a clear free body diagram for every joint or section, state your sign convention, and check one equilibrium equation you did not use.

notes.h: Stress, strain, Hooke's law and Poisson's ratio
notes.body:
Stress is internal force per unit area. Strain is deformation per unit length. Linking the two through material properties is the core of stress analysis.

Direct (normal) stress and strain
- σ = P/A, acting perpendicular to the cross-section. Tensile is positive, compressive negative. Units: Pa = N/m²; in practice N/mm² = MPa.
- ε = δ/L (extension over original length), dimensionless; often quoted in microstrain (1 με = 10⁻⁶).

Shear stress and strain
- τ = F/A, where F acts parallel to the area (for example a bolt in single shear).
- Shear strain γ is the change in the originally right angle, in radians.
- Complementary shear: a shear stress on one face is always accompanied by an equal shear stress on the perpendicular faces, so the element does not rotate.

Hooke's law
For most engineering metals loaded below the limit of proportionality, stress is proportional to strain:
- σ = Eε, where E is Young's modulus;
- τ = Gγ, where G is the shear modulus.
Typical values (approximate): steel E ≈ 200–210 GPa; aluminium alloys ≈ 70 GPa; copper ≈ 120 GPa.

Poisson's ratio
A bar stretched along its axis gets thinner. Poisson's ratio is
ν = −(lateral strain)/(axial strain).
For metals ν is typically about 0.3 (approximate); rubber approaches 0.5 (nearly incompressible); the theoretical limits for an isotropic material are −1 < ν ≤ 0.5.

Worked example
A steel rod, 20 mm diameter and 1 m long, carries 50 kN tension (E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3).
- A = π × 20²/4 = 314.2 mm², so σ = 50 000/314.2 = 159.2 MPa.
- ε = σ/E = 159.2/200 000 = 7.96 × 10⁻⁴, so the extension is 0.796 mm.
- Lateral strain = −0.3 × 7.96 × 10⁻⁴ = −2.39 × 10⁻⁴, so the diameter shrinks by 0.0048 mm (4.8 μm).

Generalised Hooke's law
When stresses act in more than one direction, each causes strain in its own direction and Poisson contraction in the others (superposition):
- εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E
- εy = [σy − ν(σx + σz)]/E
- εz = [σz − ν(σx + σy)]/E
For plane stress (σz = 0), εz = −ν(σx + σy)/E is not zero.
Example: σx = 100 MPa, σy = −50 MPa, E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3 gives εx = (100 + 15)/200 000 = 5.75 × 10⁻⁴ and εy = (−50 − 30)/200 000 = −4.0 × 10⁻⁴. Notice the compressive σy makes εx larger than σx/E alone.

Strain gauges (applied context)
A bonded resistance strain gauge measures surface strain in one direction. Two gauges at right angles on a plane-stress surface give εx and εy; inverting the equations above gives the stresses:
- σx = E(εx + νεy)/(1 − ν²)
- σy = E(εy + νεx)/(1 − ν²)

Exam tips: always convert to consistent units (N and mm give MPa directly), and remember the Poisson terms whenever there is more than one stress.

notes.h: Elastic moduli and axially loaded members
notes.body:
Young's modulus E measures stiffness in tension or compression. For an isotropic linear-elastic material only two elastic constants are independent; the others follow from them.

Relationships between the constants
- Shear modulus: G = E/[2(1 + ν)]
- Bulk modulus: K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)], where volumetric strain = −p/K under hydrostatic pressure p.
For steel (E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3): G = 200/2.6 = 76.9 GPa and K = 200/1.2 = 166.7 GPa. As ν → 0.5, K → ∞ (incompressible).
Volumetric strain for small strains: εv = εx + εy + εz.

Measuring E
In a tensile test, E is the slope of the initial straight part of the stress–strain curve. Below the limit of proportionality the material returns to its original length on unloading (elastic behaviour). Above the yield point, permanent (plastic) strain remains.

Bars in series and in parallel
- Bar of uniform section: δ = PL/(AE). The axial stiffness is k = AE/L.
- Stepped bar (segments in series): the same force passes through each segment, so δ = Σ PLᵢ/(AᵢEᵢ).
- Compound bar (parts in parallel, for example a steel core inside an aluminium tube, joined at the ends): the parts share the same strain and the loads add.
  Compatibility: ε₁ = ε₂ = ε. Equilibrium: σ₁A₁ + σ₂A₂ = P. Hence ε = P/(E₁A₁ + E₂A₂).
Example: steel (A = 500 mm², E = 200 GPa) and aluminium (A = 1000 mm², E = 70 GPa) carry 100 kN together. ε = 100 000/(1.0 × 10⁸ + 0.7 × 10⁸) = 5.88 × 10⁻⁴, so σ_steel = 117.6 MPa and σ_al = 41.2 MPa. Check: 117.6 × 500 + 41.2 × 1000 ≈ 100 kN. The stiffer material carries the higher stress.

Statically indeterminate bars
When there are more unknown forces than equilibrium equations, add a compatibility condition (how the deformations must fit together) and the load–deflection law for each part. This three-step pattern (equilibrium, compatibility, constitutive law) is the general method for indeterminate problems.

Thermal stress (applied context)
A free bar heated by ΔT grows by αLΔT. If the ends are fully restrained, a stress σ = −EαΔT develops (compressive on heating).
Example: steel, α ≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K, E = 200 GPa, heated by 50 K between rigid walls: σ = 200 000 × 12 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 = 120 MPa compression. In a compound bar of two materials with different α, heating puts the higher-α material into compression and the other into tension, with the net force zero.

Strain energy (background)
A linear-elastic bar stores energy U = ½Pδ = P²L/(2AE), or ½σε per unit volume.

Exam tips: for compound or restrained bars always write equilibrium, compatibility and Hooke's law as three separate labelled steps; most lost marks come from mixing them up.

notes.h: Thin-walled cylinders and spheres under pressure
notes.body:
Pressure vessels (boilers, gas bottles, pipes, aircraft fuselages) are analysed with thin-wall theory when the wall thickness t is small compared with the radius r. A common rule of thumb is t/r less than about 1/10 (approximate); then the stress through the wall can be treated as uniform and radial stress (which varies from −p to 0) is neglected.

Hoop (circumferential) stress in a cylinder
Cut the cylinder along its length and consider half of it, length L. The pressure pushes the two halves apart with force p × 2r × L (pressure times projected area). This is resisted by the two cut walls, each of area tL:
σh × 2tL = p × 2rL, so σh = pr/t.

Axial (longitudinal) stress in a closed cylinder
Cut across the cylinder. The pressure on the end cap gives force pπr², resisted by the wall ring of area ≈ 2πrt:
σa = pr/(2t).
So in a closed cylinder the hoop stress is twice the axial stress. This is why an over-pressurised cylinder (or a frozen water pipe) splits along its length.

Thin sphere
Any cut through the centre gives the same balance as the cylinder end: σ = pr/(2t) in every tangential direction. A sphere therefore needs only half the wall thickness of a cylinder of the same radius for the same maximum stress.

Strains and dimensional changes
The wall is in biaxial stress (σh, σa), so use the generalised Hooke's law:
- εh = (σh − νσa)/E = (pr/2tE)(2 − ν)
- εa = (σa − νσh)/E = (pr/2tE)(1 − 2ν)
- change in diameter ΔD = εh D; change in length ΔL = εa L
- volumetric strain of the contents space εv = 2εh + εa
For a sphere: ε = (pr/2tE)(1 − ν) in every direction and εv = 3ε.

Worked example
A closed steel cylinder: mean diameter 1 m, t = 10 mm, internal gauge pressure p = 2 MPa, E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3.
- σh = 2 × 500/10 = 100 MPa; σa = 50 MPa.
- εh = (100 − 15)/200 000 = 4.25 × 10⁻⁴, so the diameter grows by 0.425 mm.
- εa = (50 − 30)/200 000 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴.
- εv = 2 × 4.25 × 10⁻⁴ + 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 9.5 × 10⁻⁴.
A sphere of the same diameter and thickness at 2 MPa would have σ = 50 MPa.

Design points
- Allowable pressure for a cylinder: p = σ_allow t/r, set by the hoop stress.
- Welded or riveted seams may be weaker than the plate; a joint efficiency factor reduces the allowable stress on the seam (longitudinal seams carry hoop stress, circumferential seams carry axial stress) (background).
- Use the gauge pressure (internal minus external).

Exam tips: derive σh and σa from free body diagrams if asked, not just quote them; then remember the Poisson term when finding changes in diameter or volume.

notes.h: Shear force and bending moment in beams
notes.body:
A beam carries loads transverse to its axis. At any section the internal forces are a shear force V and a bending moment M. Shear force and bending moment diagrams (SFD and BMD) show how these vary along the beam and locate the critical section for design.

Supports and loads
- Pin: resists horizontal and vertical force. Roller: vertical force only. Built-in (fixed/encastré): two forces and a moment.
- A simply supported beam (pin + roller) and a cantilever (one built-in end) are statically determinate.
- Loads: point loads (kN), uniformly distributed loads w (kN/m), and applied couples (kN m).

Sign convention (state it in exams)
A common convention: bending moment is positive when sagging (beam concave upwards, tension at the bottom). Shear force sign conventions vary between textbooks; be consistent and state yours.

Finding V and M
1. Find reactions from equilibrium of the whole beam.
2. Cut the beam at distance x, draw a free body of one side, and write V(x) and M(x) from equilibrium.
3. Repeat for each segment between changes of loading.

Differential relationships (with w taken positive downward and V defined so that dM/dx = V)
- dM/dx = V: the slope of the BMD equals the shear force, so M is a maximum or minimum where V = 0 (or changes sign at a point load).
- dV/dx = −w: the slope of the SFD equals minus the distributed load.
- A point load causes a jump in V; an applied couple causes a jump in M.
- Under no load V is constant and M linear; under a UDL V is linear and M parabolic.

Standard results
- Simply supported, central point load P: reactions P/2; M_max = PL/4 at mid-span.
- Simply supported, UDL w over span L: reactions wL/2; M_max = wL²/8 at mid-span.
- Cantilever, end load P: M_max = PL (hogging) at the support.
- Cantilever, UDL w: M_max = wL²/2 at the support.

Worked example
A 6 m simply supported beam carries 20 kN at 2 m from the left support A.
- Moments about B: R_A × 6 = 20 × 4, so R_A = 13.33 kN; R_B = 6.67 kN.
- V = +13.33 kN from A to the load, then −6.67 kN to B.
- M rises linearly from 0 at A to 13.33 × 2 = 26.67 kN m under the load, then falls linearly to 0 at B.
The maximum moment is under the load, where the shear force changes sign.

Exam tips: check that your BMD is zero at pins, rollers and free ends (unless a couple acts there), and that the area under the SFD between two points equals the change in bending moment.

notes.h: Bending stress: the engineers' theory of bending
notes.body:
A bending moment makes one side of a beam stretch and the other shorten. The engineers' (simple) theory of bending predicts the resulting direct stress.

Assumptions
- The beam is initially straight, with a uniform cross-section symmetric about the plane of bending.
- Plane sections remain plane after bending.
- The material is linear elastic, with the same E in tension and compression.
- Bending is pure (or shear deformation is negligible) and stresses stay below the limit of proportionality.

Geometry of bending
A beam bent to radius R has a neutral surface whose length does not change. A fibre at distance y from it has strain ε = y/R. With Hooke's law, σ = Ey/R: stress varies linearly with distance from the neutral axis.

Locating the neutral axis
Zero net axial force (∫σ dA = 0) means ∫y dA = 0: the neutral axis passes through the centroid of the section.

Moment equilibrium
M = ∫σy dA = (E/R)∫y² dA = EI/R, where I = ∫y² dA is the second moment of area about the neutral axis. Together:
M/I = σ/y = E/R.

Second moments of area
- Rectangle b wide and d deep (about its centroid): I = bd³/12.
- Solid circle of diameter d: I = πd⁴/64.
- Parallel axis theorem: I about any parallel axis = I_centroid + Ah², where h is the distance between the axes.
- For an I-section, subtract the "missing" rectangles: I = BD³/12 − (B − t_w)d_w³/12.
Depth matters most: doubling d multiplies I by eight. That is why beams are deep and why I-sections put material in the flanges, far from the neutral axis.

Maximum stress and section modulus
σ_max = M y_max/I = M/Z, where Z = I/y_max is the elastic section modulus. For a rectangle, Z = bd²/6.

Worked example
A timber beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries M = 10 kN m. Take E = 10 GPa (approximate for timber).
- I = 100 × 200³/12 = 6.67 × 10⁷ mm⁴.
- σ_max = 10 × 10⁶ × 100/6.67 × 10⁷ = 15 MPa, tension at one face and compression at the other.
- Radius of curvature R = EI/M = 10 000 × 6.67 × 10⁷/10⁷ mm = 66.7 m.

Unsymmetrical sections about the bending axis
For a T-section the neutral axis is not at mid-depth, so the extreme fibre distances differ. Find the centroid first (ȳ = ΣAᵢyᵢ/ΣAᵢ), then I by the parallel axis theorem, then check both extreme fibres. This matters for materials such as cast iron or concrete that are much weaker in tension than compression.

Exam tips: keep units consistent (N, mm, MPa); always say which face is in tension; and for composite or T-sections show the centroid and parallel-axis working clearly, as most marks are for method.

Stiffness often governs beam design as much as strength: floors must not sag visibly and machine shafts must stay aligned. Deflection follows from the bending equation.

The differential equation of the elastic line
For small slopes the curvature 1/R ≈ d²v/dx², where v is the deflection. With M/I = E/R:
EI d²v/dx² = M(x)
(here v is measured upward and sagging M is positive). Integrating once gives the slope dv/dx; integrating again gives the deflection. The two constants of integration come from boundary conditions:
- pin or roller: v = 0;
- built-in end: v = 0 and dv/dx = 0;
- symmetry: dv/dx = 0 at the line of symmetry.

Example: cantilever with end load
Take x from the built-in end. M(x) = −P(L − x) (hogging). EI v″ = −P(L − x). Integrate with v(0) = v′(0) = 0:
EI v′ = −P(Lx − x²/2), EI v = −P(Lx²/2 − x³/6).
At the tip, v = −PL³/(3EI) (downward) and the slope is −PL²/(2EI).

Standard results (magnitudes)
- Cantilever, end load P: δ = PL³/(3EI), tip slope PL²/(2EI).
- Cantilever, UDL w: δ = wL⁴/(8EI), tip slope wL³/(6EI).
- Simply supported, central point load: δ = PL³/(48EI) at mid-span.
- Simply supported, UDL: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI) at mid-span.
For several loads on a linear-elastic beam, add the deflections from each load (superposition).

Macaulay's method
When point loads make M(x) change form along the beam, write one expression using Macaulay brackets ⟨x − a⟩, which equal zero when x < a and (x − a) when x ≥ a. Integrate the brackets as whole terms, ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ → ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1), and the same two constants of integration then hold along the whole beam.

Worked example
A simply supported steel beam, span 4 m, I = 2 × 10⁷ mm⁴, E = 200 GPa, carries a UDL of 5 kN/m (= 5 N/mm):
δ = 5 × 5 × 4000⁴/(384 × 200 000 × 2 × 10⁷) = 4.17 mm.
A common serviceability check for floor beams is a limit such as span/360 (here 11.1 mm); actual limits depend on the design code (background).

What controls deflection
- δ ∝ L³ (point load) or L⁴ (UDL): span is by far the strongest influence.
- δ ∝ 1/EI: flexural rigidity EI combines material and section shape.
- Changing from aluminium to steel (E ≈ 70 to 200 GPa) cuts deflection by a factor of almost three; doubling depth cuts it by eight.

Exam tips: state your sign convention and boundary conditions before integrating, keep Macaulay brackets intact while integrating, and check your answer against the standard formula when the loading is a standard case.

cards.b: A pin-ended bar loaded only at its ends: the two end forces must be equal, opposite and along the bar, so it carries pure axial tension or compression.

cards.f: Determinacy condition for a plane pin-jointed frame
cards.b: m + r = 2j (members + reaction components = 2 × joints). Greater means statically indeterminate; less means a mechanism. Necessary but not sufficient.
Find reactions, then apply ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at each joint in turn, starting where there are no more than two unknown bar forces.
Cut through at most three unknown bars and apply three equilibrium equations to one part; moments about the meeting point of two cut bars give the third force directly.
Assume every bar is in tension (force pulling away from the joint). A negative result means the bar is in compression.
At an unloaded joint with three bars, two of them collinear, the non-collinear bar carries zero force.
Frictionless pinned joints, straight bars, loads applied only at joints and self-weight neglected or lumped at joints.
σ = P/A: normal force per unit area, acting perpendicular to the section. Tension positive. 1 N/mm² = 1 MPa.
ε = δ/L: change in length divided by original length. Dimensionless; 1 microstrain = 10⁻⁶.
ν = −lateral strain/axial strain under uniaxial stress. About 0.3 for metals (approximate); 0.5 for an incompressible material.
εx = [σx − ν(σy + σz)]/E: strain from the stress in x, minus Poisson contraction from the other two stresses.
Shear stress on one plane is accompanied by equal shear stress on the perpendicular plane, so the element is in moment equilibrium.
The change, in radians, of an angle that was originally a right angle. Hooke's law in shear: τ = Gγ.
σx = E(εx + νεy)/(1 − ν²), from inverting the generalised Hooke's law with σz = 0.

cards.f: Shear modulus in terms of E and ν
cards.b: G = E/[2(1 + ν)]. For steel with E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3, G ≈ 77 GPa.

cards.f: Bulk modulus in terms of E and ν
cards.b: K = E/[3(1 − 2ν)]; it tends to infinity as ν → 0.5 (incompressible material).
δ = PL/(AE); the axial stiffness is k = AE/L.
Parts joined at the ends share the same strain, so ε = P/(E₁A₁ + E₂A₂) and σᵢ = Eᵢε.

cards.f: Thermal stress in a fully restrained bar
cards.b: σ = −EαΔT (compressive when heated); the length change αLΔT is fully suppressed.

cards.f: Three ingredients for an indeterminate problem
cards.b: Equilibrium (forces balance), compatibility (deformations fit together) and the constitutive law (Hooke's law linking force and deformation).
εv = εx + εy + εz = ΔV/V.

cards.f: Hoop stress in a thin cylinder
cards.b: σh = pr/t, from balancing pressure on the projected area 2rL against two wall sections of area tL.

cards.f: Axial stress in a closed thin cylinder
cards.b: σa = pr/(2t): end-cap force pπr² over wall area 2πrt. Half the hoop stress.
σ = pr/(2t) in all tangential directions, so a sphere needs half the thickness of a cylinder of the same radius.

cards.f: Hoop strain in a closed thin cylinder
cards.b: εh = (σh − νσa)/E = (pr/2tE)(2 − ν).

cards.f: Volumetric strain of a thin cylinder
cards.b: εv = 2εh + εa (two hoop directions contribute through the area πr², one axial through the length).
t much smaller than r (rule of thumb t/r < 1/10): wall stress uniform through the thickness and radial stress neglected.
Hoop stress pr/t is twice the axial stress pr/2t, so the hoop direction fails first, opening a crack along the length.
Moment that bends the beam concave upwards, with tension in the bottom fibres; commonly taken as positive.
dM/dx = V: the slope of the bending moment diagram equals the shear force, so M peaks where V is zero or changes sign.

cards.f: Relation between V and distributed load
cards.b: dV/dx = −w (w downward positive): the SFD slopes at the load intensity; under no load V is constant.

cards.f: Maximum BM: simply supported beam, UDL
cards.b: M_max = wL²/8 at mid-span, with reactions wL/2.

cards.f: Maximum BM: simply supported beam, central point load
cards.b: M_max = PL/4 at mid-span.
M_max = wL²/2 (hogging) at the built-in end.

cards.f: Effect of a point load on the SFD and BMD
cards.b: A step in the SFD equal to the load, and a kink (change of slope) in the BMD.
M/I = σ/y = E/R: moment, second moment of area, stress at distance y from the neutral axis, Young's modulus and radius of curvature.

cards.f: Where is the neutral axis in elastic bending?
cards.b: Through the centroid of the cross-section, because the net axial force ∫σ dA must be zero.

cards.f: Second moment of area of a rectangle
cards.b: I = bd³/12 about the centroidal axis parallel to b (d is the depth in the direction of bending).

cards.f: Second moment of area of a solid circle
cards.b: I = πd⁴/64 about a diameter.
I_xx = I_c + Ah²: second moment about any axis equals that about the parallel centroidal axis plus area times distance squared.
Z = I/y_max, so σ_max = M/Z. For a rectangle Z = bd²/6.
Cross-sections that are plane before bending remain plane after, giving a strain that varies linearly with y: ε = y/R.

cards.f: Differential equation of the elastic line
cards.b: EI d²v/dx² = M(x) for small slopes; integrate twice and use boundary conditions to find slope and deflection.

cards.f: Tip deflection: cantilever with end load
cards.b: δ = PL³/(3EI); tip slope = PL²/(2EI).
δ = wL⁴/(8EI).

cards.f: Mid-span deflection: simply supported, central load
cards.b: δ = PL³/(48EI).
δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI).
Zero for x < a and (x − a) for x ≥ a; integrated as a whole term so one set of constants applies along the beam.

cards.f: Boundary conditions at a built-in end
cards.b: Deflection v = 0 and slope dv/dx = 0.
For linear-elastic, small-deflection beams the deflection under several loads is the sum of those caused by each load alone.

questions.q: A plane pin-jointed frame has 9 joints, 15 members and is supported by a pin and a roller (3 reaction components). How is it classified by the counting rule?
options: Statically indeterminate to the first degree
A mechanism with three degrees of freedom
It cannot be classified without knowing the loads
questions.why: m + r = 15 + 3 = 18 and 2j = 2 × 9 = 18, so the counting rule gives a statically determinate frame. 'Indeterminate to the first degree' comes from treating the roller as a pin (r = 4, so m + r = 19). 'A mechanism with three degrees of freedom' comes from counting only the 15 members against the 18 joint equations and forgetting the 3 reactions. Determinacy depends on the members, joints and supports, not on the loads, so the frame can be classified without them.

questions.q: A symmetric triangular frame has a pin at A and a roller at B, 4 m apart, with apex C 2 m above the mid-point of AB. A 10 kN vertical load acts downward at C. What is the force in bar AC?
questions.why: Each support carries 5 kN. At A, vertical equilibrium gives F_AC sin 45° = −5, so F_AC = −5/0.707 = −7.07 kN: 7.07 kN compression. The same magnitude in tension has the wrong sense: the upward reaction must be balanced by AC pushing on the joint. 5.00 kN is the reaction itself, forgetting to divide by sin 45°. 10.0 kN is the whole applied load, ignoring that it is shared between two inclined bars.

questions.q: A Warren truss of equilateral triangles with 2 m sides spans 6 m between a pin at A and a roller at D. Bottom joints B and C are at 2 m and 4 m from A; top joints E, F, G are at x = 1, 3 and 5 m. A single 12 kN load acts downward at B. Use the method of sections to find the forces in top chord EF, diagonal BF and bottom chord BC.
markScheme: Reactions R_A = 8 kN and R_D = 4 kN from moments about A and D
Section cut through EF, BF and BC with a free body of the left part
F_BC = (8 × 3 − 12 × 1)/√3 = 6.93 kN tension (moments about F)
F_EF = −(8 × 2)/√3 = −9.24 kN, i.e. compression (moments about B)
F_BF = 4/sin 60° = 4.62 kN tension (vertical equilibrium)
questions.modelAnswer: Whole truss: moments about D give R_A × 6 = 12 × 4, so R_A = 8 kN; then R_D = 12 − 8 = 4 kN. Cut through EF, BF and BC and keep the left part (R_A, the 12 kN load at B and the three bar forces, all assumed tensile). The height is 2 sin 60° = 1.732 m. Moments about F (x = 3, y = 1.732): F_BC × 1.732 = 8 × 3 − 12 × 1 = 12, so F_BC = 6.93 kN tension. Moments about B (x = 2, y = 0), where BF and BC pass through B: F_EF × 1.732 + 8 × 2 = 0, so F_EF = −9.24 kN, i.e. 9.24 kN compression. Vertical equilibrium: 8 − 12 + F_BF sin 60° = 0, so F_BF = 4/0.866 = 4.62 kN tension.

questions.q: A steel rod 20 mm in diameter and 1 m long carries an axial tension of 50 kN. With E = 200 GPa, what is its extension?
questions.why: σ = 50 000/(π × 10²) = 159.2 MPa, ε = 159.2/200 000 = 7.96 × 10⁻⁴, so δ = εL = 0.796 mm ≈ 0.80 mm. 0.20 mm comes from treating the 20 mm diameter as the radius (area π × 20² = 1257 mm², four times too big). 3.18 mm comes from putting the 10 mm radius into πd²/4 (area 78.5 mm², four times too small). 0.24 mm is the extension multiplied by Poisson's ratio (0.3 × 0.796), which mixes up the lateral strain with the axial extension.

questions.q: A thin plate (plane stress) has σx = 100 MPa and σy = −50 MPa. With E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3, what is the strain εx?
questions.why: εx = (σx − νσy)/E = (100 − 0.3 × (−50))/200 000 = 115/200 000 = 5.75 × 10⁻⁴. 4.25 × 10⁻⁴ results from dropping the minus sign on σy (using +50 MPa), giving (100 − 15)/E. 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ is σx/E, ignoring the Poisson effect of σy. −4.00 × 10⁻⁴ is εy = (σy − νσx)/E, the strain in the other direction.

questions.q: Two strain gauges are bonded at right angles on the free surface of an aluminium component (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33). They read εx = 600 με and εy = −100 με. Find σx and σy, and the through-thickness strain εz.
markScheme: Recognises plane stress (σz = 0) and inverts Hooke's law: σx = E(εx + νεy)/(1 − ν²)
σx ≈ 44.5 MPa
σy = E(εy + νεx)/(1 − ν²) ≈ 7.7 MPa
εz = −ν(σx + σy)/E ≈ −246 με
Consistent units and sign conventions
questions.modelAnswer: The surface is free, so σz = 0. Inverting the generalised Hooke's law: σx = E(εx + νεy)/(1 − ν²) = 70 000 × (600 − 33) × 10⁻⁶/(1 − 0.1089) = 70 000 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁴/0.8911 = 44.5 MPa. σy = E(εy + νεx)/(1 − ν²) = 70 000 × (−100 + 198) × 10⁻⁶/0.8911 = 7.7 MPa. Through the thickness, εz = −ν(σx + σy)/E = −0.33 × 52.2/70 000 = −2.46 × 10⁻⁴, i.e. about −246 με: the plate gets thinner even though no stress acts in z.

questions.q: A material has E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3. What is its shear modulus G?
questions.why: G = E/[2(1 + ν)] = 200/2.6 = 76.9 GPa. 153.8 GPa is E/(1 + ν), forgetting the factor of 2. 166.7 GPa is the bulk modulus E/[3(1 − 2ν)], a different constant. 71.4 GPa is E/[2(1 + 2ν)] = 200/2.8, i.e. using 2ν in place of ν (confusing the shear-modulus formula with the 1 − 2ν term in the bulk modulus).

questions.q: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa, α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K) is fixed between rigid walls with zero initial stress and then heated by 50 K. What stress develops?
options: 0 MPa, because the bar is free to expand
questions.why: The suppressed thermal strain is αΔT = 6 × 10⁻⁴, so σ = EαΔT = 200 000 MPa × 6 × 10⁻⁴ = 120 MPa, and it is compressive because the walls push back on a bar that wants to lengthen. Tension would arise on cooling, not heating. 0.12 MPa comes from entering E as 200 (its value in GPa) and then reading the result, 0.12 GPa, as if it were in MPa. Zero stress would apply only to an unrestrained bar, but here the walls are rigid.

questions.q: A short column is a steel rod (area 500 mm², E = 200 GPa) inside an aluminium tube (area 1000 mm², E = 70 GPa), both the same length and loaded through rigid end plates by 100 kN compression. Find the stress in each material and the share of the load each carries.
markScheme: Compatibility: both parts have the same strain
Equilibrium: σ_s A_s + σ_a A_a = 100 kN
σ_steel = 117.6 MPa, σ_al = 41.2 MPa (both compressive)
Loads: steel 58.8 kN, aluminium 41.2 kN, summing to 100 kN
questions.modelAnswer: Because the end plates are rigid, both parts shorten by the same amount, so they have equal strain ε. Equilibrium: E_s ε A_s + E_a ε A_a = P, so ε = 100 000/(200 000 × 500 + 70 000 × 1000) = 100 000/1.7 × 10⁸ = 5.88 × 10⁻⁴. Stresses: σ_s = 200 000 × 5.88 × 10⁻⁴ = 117.6 MPa and σ_a = 70 000 × 5.88 × 10⁻⁴ = 41.2 MPa, both compressive. Loads: steel 117.6 × 500 = 58.8 kN, aluminium 41.2 × 1000 = 41.2 kN; total 100 kN, as required. The steel carries more load from half the area because it is nearly three times stiffer.

questions.q: A closed thin cylinder of mean diameter 1 m and wall thickness 10 mm holds gas at a gauge pressure of 2 MPa. What is the hoop stress?
questions.why: σh = pr/t = 2 × 500/10 = 100 MPa. 50 MPa is pr/(2t), the axial stress (or the stress in a sphere). 200 MPa puts the diameter instead of the radius into pr/t. 0.04 MPa inverts the geometry ratio, calculating pt/r = 2 × 10/500.

questions.q: A thin spherical vessel of mean diameter 1 m must hold a gauge pressure of 2 MPa with a wall stress no greater than 100 MPa. What minimum wall thickness is needed?
questions.why: For a sphere σ = pr/(2t), so t = pr/(2σ) = 2 × 500/(2 × 100) = 5 mm. 10 mm comes from using the cylinder hoop formula t = pr/σ, which does not apply to a sphere (it is also what you get by putting the diameter into the sphere formula). 20 mm uses the hoop formula with the diameter instead of the radius. 50 mm comes from entering the pressure as 20 (its value in bar) instead of 2 MPa in the correct sphere formula.

questions.q: Show that the hoop strain in a closed thin cylinder is εh = (pr/2tE)(2 − ν). For p = 2 MPa, r = 500 mm, t = 10 mm, E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3, find the change in diameter and the volumetric strain.
markScheme: Uses σh = pr/t and σa = pr/(2t)
εh = (σh − νσa)/E = (pr/tE)(1 − ν/2) = (pr/2tE)(2 − ν)
questions.modelAnswer: The wall is in biaxial stress with σh = pr/t and σa = pr/(2t). Hooke's law with Poisson's effect gives εh = (σh − νσa)/E = (pr/tE) − ν(pr/2tE) = (pr/2tE)(2 − ν). Numerically pr/(2tE) = 2 × 500/(2 × 10 × 200 000) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴, so εh = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 1.7 = 4.25 × 10⁻⁴ and ΔD = 4.25 × 10⁻⁴ × 1000 = 0.425 mm. Axially, εa = (pr/2tE)(1 − 2ν) = 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.4 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴. The internal volume is πr²L, so εv = 2εh + εa = 8.5 × 10⁻⁴ + 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 9.5 × 10⁻⁴.

questions.q: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a single 20 kN point load 2 m from the left support. What is the maximum bending moment?
questions.why: R_A = 20 × 4/6 = 13.33 kN, and the maximum moment is under the load: 13.33 × 2 = 26.7 kN m (equivalently Pab/L = 20 × 2 × 4/6). 30.0 kN m is PL/4, valid only for a central load. 40.0 kN m is the load times its 2 m distance from A, as if the load were on a cantilever with no reaction. 13.3 kN m is the smaller reaction R_B = 6.67 kN multiplied by 2 m, pairing a reaction with the wrong lever arm (R_B is 4 m from the load).

questions.q: Along a portion of a beam carrying a uniformly distributed load and no point loads, what are the shapes of the shear force and bending moment diagrams?
options: Shear force linear, bending moment parabolic
Shear force constant, bending moment linear
Shear force parabolic, bending moment cubic
Shear force zero, bending moment constant
questions.why: dV/dx = −w with w constant makes V linear, and dM/dx = V then makes M quadratic (parabolic). 'Constant and linear' describes an unloaded portion. 'Parabolic and cubic' is the pattern under a linearly varying (triangular) load. 'Zero and constant' is pure bending, for example between the two loads of a four-point bend test.

questions.q: A cantilever of length 3 m carries a UDL of 4 kN/m along its whole length and a 10 kN point load at its free end. Find the shear force and bending moment at the built-in end, and sketch the shape of each diagram.
markScheme: Shear at the support = 4 × 3 + 10 = 22 kN
Moment at the support = 4 × 3²/2 + 10 × 3 = 18 + 30 = 48 kN m (hogging)
SFD linear from 10 kN at the free end to 22 kN at the support
BMD parabolic, zero at the free end, maximum magnitude at the support
questions.modelAnswer: Take a section at distance x from the free end. V(x) = 10 + 4x (kN), so V rises linearly from 10 kN at the tip to 22 kN at the support. M(x) = −(10x + 4x²/2) = −(10x + 2x²) kN m (hogging, so negative in the sagging-positive convention). At the support (x = 3): |M| = 30 + 18 = 48 kN m. The SFD is a straight sloping line. The BMD is a parabola that starts at zero at the tip (with a slope equal to the 10 kN tip shear) and grows to 48 kN m hogging at the wall.

questions.q: A rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries a bending moment of 10 kN m about its horizontal axis. What is the maximum bending stress?
questions.why: I = 100 × 200³/12 = 6.67 × 10⁷ mm⁴ and σ = My/I = 10⁷ × 100/6.67 × 10⁷ = 15 MPa (equivalently M/Z with Z = bd²/6). 30 MPa uses the full depth (200 mm) as y instead of the 100 mm from the neutral axis to the extreme fibre. 7.5 MPa uses I = bd³/6, double the correct value. 1.25 MPa omits the 12 in bd³/12, making I twelve times too large.

questions.q: If the depth of a solid rectangular beam is doubled while its width and the applied moment stay the same, what happens to the maximum bending stress?
questions.why: σ_max = M/Z with Z = bd²/6, so doubling d multiplies Z by 4 and divides the stress by 4. 'One eighth' is the change in curvature or deflection, which depend on I = bd³/12 (×8), not on Z. 'Halves' would be true if Z depended linearly on d. 'Unchanged' ignores that the section is stronger.

questions.q: A T-section has a flange 100 mm wide × 20 mm thick on top of a web 20 mm thick × 100 mm deep (total depth 120 mm). Find the height of the neutral axis above the base and the second moment of area about it. Hence find the maximum tensile and compressive stresses for a sagging moment of 5 kN m.
markScheme: Areas 2000 mm² (flange, centroid 110 mm above base) and 2000 mm² (web, centroid 50 mm)
Sagging: bottom fibre (80 mm from NA) in tension: σ = 5 × 10⁶ × 80/5.33 × 10⁶ = 75.0 MPa
Top fibre (40 mm from NA) in compression: 37.5 MPa
questions.modelAnswer: Measure y from the base. Flange: A = 100 × 20 = 2000 mm², centroid at 110 mm. Web: A = 20 × 100 = 2000 mm², centroid at 50 mm. ȳ = (2000 × 110 + 2000 × 50)/4000 = 80 mm. Parallel axis theorem: flange I = 100 × 20³/12 + 2000 × (110 − 80)² = 66 667 + 1 800 000 = 1 866 667 mm⁴; web I = 20 × 100³/12 + 2000 × (80 − 50)² = 1 666 667 + 1 800 000 = 3 466 667 mm⁴. Total I = 5.33 × 10⁶ mm⁴. In sagging the bottom is in tension: y = 80 mm, σ = 5 × 10⁶ × 80/5.33 × 10⁶ = 75.0 MPa tension. The top is 40 mm above the NA: σ = 5 × 10⁶ × 40/5.33 × 10⁶ = 37.5 MPa compression.

questions.q: The span of a simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load (same load per metre) is doubled. By what factor does the mid-span deflection increase?
questions.why: δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI) with w fixed, so δ ∝ L⁴ and doubling L gives 2⁴ = 16. A factor of 8 is the L³ dependence that applies to a point load. A factor of 4 is how the maximum bending moment wL²/8 scales. A factor of 2 would assume deflection grows only in proportion to span.

questions.q: A steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa, I = 8 × 10⁶ mm⁴) of length 2 m carries a 5 kN load at its tip. What is the tip deflection?
questions.why: δ = PL³/(3EI) = 5000 × 2000³/(3 × 200 000 × 8 × 10⁶) = 4 × 10¹³/4.8 × 10¹² = 8.33 mm. 25.0 mm omits the factor of 3 in the denominator. 12.5 mm uses 2EI as the denominator, borrowing the 2 from the tip-slope formula PL²/(2EI). 0.52 mm uses PL³/(48EI), the simply supported central-load result.

questions.q: Starting from EI v″ = M, derive the tip deflection of a cantilever of length L carrying a point load P at its free end. State your boundary conditions.
markScheme: M(x) = −P(L − x) with x from the built-in end (hogging negative)
First integration: EI v′ = −P(Lx − x²/2) + C₁, with v′(0) = 0 so C₁ = 0
Second integration: EI v = −P(Lx²/2 − x³/6) + C₂, with v(0) = 0 so C₂ = 0
At x = L: v = −PL³/(3EI), i.e. PL³/(3EI) downward
Clear sign convention stated
questions.modelAnswer: Measure x from the built-in end and v upward; sagging moments positive. A section at x has the load P at distance (L − x), giving a hogging moment M = −P(L − x). EI v″ = −PL + Px. Integrating: EI v′ = −PLx + Px²/2 + C₁. At the built-in end the slope is zero, so C₁ = 0. Integrating again: EI v = −PLx²/2 + Px³/6 + C₂; v(0) = 0 so C₂ = 0. At the tip x = L: EI v = −PL³/2 + PL³/6 = −PL³/3, so v_tip = −PL³/(3EI): a downward deflection of PL³/(3EI). The tip slope is −PL²/(2EI).

questions.q:
A closed-ended thin-walled steel cylinder has a mean diameter of 800 mm, wall thickness 8 mm and length 2 m. It is filled with fluid at an internal gauge pressure of 3 MPa. Take E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.3.
(a) Derive expressions for the hoop and axial stresses and evaluate them. [6]
(b) Find the hoop and axial strains and the changes in diameter and length. [6]
(c) Find the increase in internal volume (ignore the end caps' own deformation). [4]
(d) The material's allowable stress is 120 MPa. What is the maximum safe pressure, and what thickness would hemispherical end caps of the same radius need at that pressure for the same allowable stress? [4]
markScheme: (a) Free body diagrams: σh = pr/t = 3 × 400/8 = 150 MPa; σa = pr/(2t) = 75 MPa
(c) V = π × 0.4² × 2 = 1.005 m³, so ΔV ≈ 1.43 × 10⁻³ m³ (about 1.43 litres)
(d) Hoop stress governs: p_max = 120 × 8/400 = 2.4 MPa
(d) Hemisphere: σ = pr/(2t) gives t = 2.4 × 400/(2 × 120) = 4 mm
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Cut the cylinder lengthways: the pressure on the projected area 2rL is balanced by hoop stress on two wall sections of area tL, so σh = pr/t = 3 × 400/8 = 150 MPa. Cut across it: the pressure force on the end, pπr², is balanced by axial stress on the wall ring of area 2πrt, so σa = pr/(2t) = 75 MPa.

(b) The wall is in biaxial stress. εh = (σh − νσa)/E = (150 − 22.5)/200 000 = 6.375 × 10⁻⁴. εa = (σa − νσh)/E = (75 − 45)/200 000 = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴. Change in diameter = 6.375 × 10⁻⁴ × 800 = 0.51 mm (increase). Change in length = 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ × 2000 = 0.30 mm (increase).

(c) The volume πr²L gives εv = 2εh + εa = 1.275 × 10⁻³ + 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.425 × 10⁻³. The original volume is π × 0.4² × 2 = 1.005 m³, so ΔV = 1.425 × 10⁻³ × 1.005 = 1.43 × 10⁻³ m³, about 1.43 litres. (This is extra fluid that must be pumped in to reach 3 MPa, in addition to any compression of the fluid itself.)

(d) The hoop stress is the larger, so it governs: 120 = p × 400/8 gives p_max = 2.4 MPa. For a hemispherical end, σ = pr/(2t), so t = 2.4 × 400/(2 × 120) = 4 mm: half the cylinder wall, which is why spherical ends can be thinner (in practice, the thickness change at the joint is detailed carefully to limit local bending).

questions.q:
A simply supported steel beam AB of span 6 m carries a uniformly distributed load of 4 kN/m over its whole length (including self-weight) and a 30 kN point load 2 m from A. The beam is a symmetric I-section: flanges 150 mm × 20 mm, web 10 mm thick, overall depth 300 mm. E = 200 GPa.
(a) Find the reactions and sketch the shear force and bending moment diagrams, giving key values. [7]
(b) Find the second moment of area of the section and the maximum bending stress. [6]
(c) Use Macaulay's method to find the deflection at mid-span. [12]
markScheme: (a) SF: 32 kN at A falling linearly to 24 kN just left of the load, −6 kN just right, falling to −22 kN at B
(a) SF changes sign at the load, so M_max = 32 × 2 − 4 × 2²/2 = 56 kN m there; M = 0 at A and B
(b) σ_max = 56 × 10⁶ × 150/1.324 × 10⁸ = 63.4 MPa (compression top, tension bottom)
(c) EI v = 32x³/6 − 30⟨x − 2⟩³/6 − 4x⁴/24 + C₁x + C₂ (kN, m); v(0) = 0 gives C₂ = 0
(c) v(6) = 0 gives C₁ = −102.67 kN m²
(c) EI = 26 490 kN m²; at x = 3 m, EI v = −182.5 kN m³, so v = −6.89 mm (6.9 mm downward)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Moments about B: 6R_A = 30 × 4 + 24 × 3, so R_A = (120 + 72)/6 = 32 kN. Then R_B = 30 + 24 − 32 = 22 kN. Shear force (left-hand free body, upward positive): V = 32 − 4x for 0 < x < 2, so 32 kN at A and 24 kN just left of the load; it drops by 30 to −6 kN just right of the load, then V = 32 − 30 − 4x reaches −22 kN at B. Bending moment: M = 32x − 2x² for x ≤ 2 m, so M(2) = 64 − 8 = 56 kN m. Since V changes sign at the load, this is the maximum. Beyond the load M = 32x − 30(x − 2) − 2x², which falls to zero at B (check: 192 − 120 − 72 = 0). The BMD is made of two parabolic arcs meeting at a peak of 56 kN m under the load.

(b) I = 150 × 300³/12 − (150 − 10) × 260³/12 = 3.375 × 10⁸ − 2.051 × 10⁸ = 1.324 × 10⁸ mm⁴. With y_max = 150 mm: σ_max = 56 × 10⁶ × 150/1.324 × 10⁸ = 63.4 MPa: compressive in the top flange and tensile in the bottom flange (sagging).

(c) Using kN and m with sagging positive and v upward: EI v″ = 32x − 30⟨x − 2⟩ − 2x². Integrate: EI v′ = 16x² − 15⟨x − 2⟩² − (2/3)x³ + C₁; EI v = (16/3)x³ − 5⟨x − 2⟩³ − x⁴/6 + C₁x + C₂. At x = 0, v = 0, so C₂ = 0 (the bracket is zero there). At x = 6: 1152 − 5 × 64 − 216 + 6C₁ = 0, so 616 + 6C₁ = 0 and C₁ = −102.67 kN m². At mid-span x = 3: EI v = 144 − 5 × 1 − 13.5 − 308.0 = −182.5 kN m³. EI = 200 × 10⁶ kN/m² × 1.324 × 10⁻⁴ m⁴ = 26 490 kN m², so v = −182.5/26 490 = −6.89 × 10⁻³ m: the mid-span deflects 6.9 mm downward. (A numerical check finds the maximum deflection, about 6.92 mm, at roughly 2.83 m from A, very close to mid-span, as expected for a beam whose load is fairly evenly spread.)
